Event Viewer's Security log records logons and account changes. Key IDs: 4624 successful logon, 4625 failed logon, 4672 special (admin-level) privileges at logon, 4720 user account created, 1102 audit log cleared.
Logon types

Events 4624 and 4625 include a logon type. Type 2 is at the keyboard, 3 is over the network (like a file share) and 10 is Remote Desktop. With Network Level Authentication on, failed RDP logons often show as type 3, so check the source IP too.
SIEMs

A SIEM collects logs from many systems in one place, correlates them and raises alerts. Wazuh is a free, open-source option; Microsoft Sentinel and Splunk are common at work. Alerts only help if someone acts on them.
Red flags
Many failures then a success from the same IP. A logon at 3am from a new country. A new admin account. The Security log being cleared. Any one might be innocent; together they tell a story.
real: Target's ignored alerts, 2013

Remember Target from Day 9? Its malware detection tool raised alerts as the attackers set up, and a monitoring team overseas passed them on. The team in the US didn't act on them in time. Logging and alerting only help when someone responds.
myth: No alerts means no attacks.
It might mean you aren't collecting the right logs, or nobody has tuned the alerts. Attackers also clear logs, which is why Event ID 1102 matters.

tryit.p: Lock the Windows target and enter a wrong password three times. Then log in and pull the failures. If nothing shows, check that logon auditing is turned on.
tryit.code:
# Windows PowerShell (admin)
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625} -MaxEvents 5 |
  Format-List TimeCreated, Message

auditpol /get /subcategory:"Logon"

quiz.q: Hundreds of Event ID 4625 entries from one IP in a minute suggest what?
quiz.w: 4625 is a failed logon. A burst from one source is a classic brute-force signal.

quiz.q: Event ID 1102 appears on a server at 2am. Why worry?
o: Someone cleared the Security log, possibly to hide their tracks
quiz.w: Clearing the log is rare in normal operations and common after an intrusion. Investigate who did it.

quiz.q: Many 4625 events with logon type 10 arrive from one external IP. What's being targeted?
quiz.w: Type 10 is RemoteInteractive, which is RDP. Type 3 is usually a network logon like a file share, though with NLA on, failed RDP attempts can show as type 3 too.

quiz.q: What does OWASP Top 10:2025 call A09?
quiz.w: The 2021 name was Security Logging and Monitoring Failures. The 2025 list renamed it to stress alerting.

recap: Linux: auth.log, secure or journalctl.
Logon type 3 is network, 10 is RDP, but failed RDP often shows as 3.
A SIEM centralises logs, but someone has to act on alerts.

days.sub: Attack your own lab and see what the defender sees.
learn: The plan
You'll scan the Windows target from Kali while watching with Wireshark and the Windows firewall log. Seeing both sides of one attack is the fastest way to learn detection.
Set up
Both VMs on the labnet internal network: Kali at 10.10.10.10, Windows at 10.10.10.20. Snapshot both first. Confirm they can see each other with `sudo nmap -sn 10.10.10.0/24`.
Give the defender eyes
Windows Defender Firewall doesn't log dropped packets by default. Turn logging on (see the Try it card). The log lives at C:\Windows\System32\LogFiles\Firewall\pfirewall.log.
Run the scan
Start Wireshark on Kali's eth0, then apply the display filter `tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0`. Now run the SYN scan. Watch a wall of SYNs from one source hit many ports in seconds.
Compare the evidence

In Wireshark, Statistics then Conversations shows one source talking to many ports. On Windows, the firewall log shows a DROP line for each blocked probe. What did the scan learn, and what did the defender see?
real: A scan from the inside

SOC analysts treat scans very differently depending on where they come from. Scans from the internet are constant background noise. An internal laptop scanning the server subnet often means a compromised machine looking for its next hop.
myth: If a scan didn't show up in Event Viewer, nothing recorded it.
A SYN scan rarely creates logon events, but firewall logs, network flow records and intrusion detection systems all see it. Detection depends on looking in the right place.

tryit.p: Turn on firewall logging and tail the log on Windows. Then scan from Kali and watch the DROP lines arrive. Afterwards, restore both clean snapshots.
tryit.code:
# Windows PowerShell (admin)
Set-NetFirewallProfile -All -LogBlocked True
Get-Content C:\Windows\System32\LogFiles\Firewall\pfirewall.log -Tail 20 -Wait

# Kali
sudo nmap -sS --top-ports 200 10.10.10.20

# Windows: turn logging off again
Set-NetFirewallProfile -All -LogBlocked False

quiz.q: What pattern in Wireshark shows a port scan?
o: Many SYNs from one source to many ports
quiz.w: A scanner probes many ports fast, so you see a burst of SYNs from one IP across many destination ports.

quiz.q: Once logging is on, where does Windows Defender Firewall record dropped packets?
o: The Security log as Event ID 4625
quiz.w: The firewall writes its own text log. 4625 is a failed logon, and auth.log is on Linux.

quiz.q: Most ports on the Windows target show as filtered. What does that tell you?
o: The firewall is silently dropping the probes
The Windows VM is switched off
quiz.w: Filtered means no useful reply came back. A powered-off host would show as down, not filtered.

quiz.q: A finance laptop starts scanning the server subnet at midnight. What's the most likely explanation?
o: The laptop may be compromised and looking for its next target
quiz.w: Workstations don't scan servers in normal operations. Treat it as possible lateral movement and investigate.

recap: Snapshot first, internal network only.
Wireshark shows a burst of SYNs from one source.
Turn on firewall logging to see the drops.
Internal scanning is a lateral movement red flag.

days.t: Defence in depth and incident response
days.sub: Layers before, a plan during, lessons after.
learn: Defence in depth

Stack controls so one failure doesn't become a breach: training, MFA, patching, firewalls, segmentation, endpoint protection, logging and backups. Each layer is another chance to stop or spot an attacker.
Types of control

Preventive controls stop things, like MFA and firewalls. Detective controls spot them, like logs and alerts. Corrective controls fix things afterwards, like backups and reimaging. Good defence mixes all three.
The four-phase cycle
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 described four phases: preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; and post-incident activity. You'll still see it in textbooks and interviews.
Rev. 3 and CSF 2.0

NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (April 2025) instead organises incident response around the six CSF 2.0 functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. Preparation is now spread across Govern, Identify and Protect.
In the moment

Contain first: isolate the machine from the network, but don't switch it off, because memory holds evidence. Preserve logs, note what you do and when, and escalate. Then remove the cause and recover from clean backups.
Learn from it
After recovery, hold a blameless review and fix the gaps. If personal information was breached and serious harm is likely, report it: to the OAIC in Australia or the Privacy Commissioner in NZ.
real: Maersk and NotPetya, 2017

In June 2017 NotPetya malware tore through shipping giant Maersk, wiping thousands of machines within hours. Every domain controller was hit except one in Ghana, which happened to be offline during a power cut. That one copy let Maersk rebuild its network in about ten days.
myth: Incident response starts when you get breached.
Most of it happens before: knowing your assets, backups, logging, contacts and a written plan. Rev. 3 makes that explicit with Govern, Identify and Protect.

tryit.where: Notes app or your GitHub repo
tryit.p: Write a one-page playbook for “a user entered their password on a phishing page”. Cover who to tell, resetting the password and signing out all sessions, which logs to check, and what to tell the user.

quiz.q: What does NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 align incident response with?
quiz.w: Rev. 3 is a CSF 2.0 Community Profile, so incident response sits under the CSF functions.

quiz.q: A laptop shows signs of ransomware. What should you do first?
o: Disconnect it from the network but leave it powered on
Switch it off at the wall
quiz.w: Isolating stops the spread. Keeping it on preserves memory evidence such as running processes and keys.

quiz.q: Which of these is a detective control?
quiz.w: Alerts detect. MFA prevents, and restoring from backup corrects.

quiz.q: What are the six CSF 2.0 functions?
o: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
Prepare, Detect, Contain, Eradicate, Recover, Review
quiz.w: CSF 2.0 added Govern to the five functions of CSF 1.1.

recap: Defence in depth: many layers, no single point of failure.
Preventive, detective and corrective controls.
Rev. 2 had four phases; Rev. 3 uses the CSF 2.0 functions.
Isolate, preserve evidence, escalate, recover, then learn.

days.sub: Four weeks, one last pass.
learn: How to review
This is the big one. Answer each review card's heading out loud first. Then do the quiz cold, without scrolling back. Anything you miss tells you which day to redo.
real: Latitude Financial, 2023

In March 2023 an attack through a major vendor gave attackers a Latitude Financial employee's login. They took about 14 million Australian and NZ records, including millions of driver licence numbers, some kept since 2005. Latitude refused to pay. Third-party access and keeping too much data, in one story.
myth: Once you've finished Stage 1, the basics are done.
The basics are what most breaches exploit: missing MFA, unpatched systems, weak access control and ignored alerts. You'll use these ideas at every level.

tryit.p: From memory, write down the key ports, the Windows Event IDs, the MFA ranking, the permission octals and the six CSF 2.0 functions. Then check it against the cards. Keep it for interview prep.

review: Level B1

CIA, and double extortion hitting all three. Threats include insiders and accidents. Risk is likelihood and impact. Authorisation is checked on every request, with least privilege. SMS is MFA but weak; only FIDO2 keys and passkeys are phishing-resistant.
Level B2
Open means listening, not vulnerable. TCP has a handshake; UDP doesn't. DHCP, ARP, DNS, TCP and TLS get a laptop to a website. The padlock means encrypted, not honest.
Level B3
Config lives in /etc or the Registry. Read rwx and octal. Judge a process by its path and parent, not its name. Hash passwords with bcrypt or Argon2. Vulnerable VMs never go on bridged networks.
Level B4

Nmap finds hosts, ports and versions, with permission only. Wireshark shows the wire. Logs and a SIEM catch what attackers leave behind. Incident response now follows the CSF 2.0 functions. Defence in depth means no single control does everything.
Explain: SMS MFA
SMS counts as MFA, but SIM swapping and fake login pages can steal the code. App codes can be phished too. FIDO2 keys and passkeys check the real domain, so a phishing site gets nothing.
Explain: open ports
Open just means a service is listening. Risk depends on what it is, its version, its configuration and who can reach it. RDP open to the internet is risky; 443 on a patched web server is expected.
Explain: backups
Offline or immutable backups restore encrypted data and get you running again. They do nothing about data that's already been stolen, the other half of double extortion.
Explain: HTTPS
TLS checks the server's certificate, agrees session keys, then encrypts traffic between browser and server. The data is decrypted at the server, so stored data needs its own protection.

quiz.q: Which statement is correct?
o: An open port proves a vulnerability
A passkey resists phishing better than an SMS code
quiz.w: Passkeys are bound to the real site. The other two are misconceptions this plan set out to fix.

quiz.q: In OWASP Top 10:2025, what is A09?
quiz.w: A01 is Broken Access Control and A05 is Injection.

quiz.q: Ransomware steals data, then encrypts it. Which pillars are hit?
quiz.w: Theft breaks confidentiality, unauthorised encryption breaks integrity and lost access breaks availability.

quiz.q: Which of these is the most worrying open port?
o: RDP open to the internet on an unpatched server
443 open on a patched web server
53 open on the internal DNS server
quiz.w: The other two are expected services. Exposed, unpatched RDP is a common ransomware entry point.

quiz.q: The four-phase incident response cycle comes from which document?
quiz.w: Rev. 2 had the four phases. Rev. 3 (April 2025) organises incident response around the CSF 2.0 functions.

quiz.q: Which network mode should a deliberately vulnerable VM use?
o: NAT with port forwarding to the internet
quiz.w: Keep vulnerable machines off your real network and away from the internet.

quiz.q: A file owned by alice, group staff, is set to 640. What can a staff member who isn't alice do?
quiz.w: 6 gives the owner rw-, 4 gives the group r--, and 0 gives others nothing.

quiz.q: What does hardening mean?
o: Changing insecure defaults to shrink the attack surface
quiz.w: Hardening removes or changes what an attacker could use: default credentials, unneeded services, open ports and unused software.

recap: You can explain CIA, risk, AAA and MFA strength.
You can trace a connection from DHCP to TLS.
You can read permissions, processes, hashes and logs.
Score 80% or more across all days before moving to intermediate.

days.sub: From fundamentals to a job-ready portfolio.
learn: What you've covered
Security fundamentals, networking, operating systems, cryptography, scanning, packet capture and logs. That's the base every intermediate topic builds on.
The intermediate stage
Next comes frameworks in depth (NIST CSF 2.0, ISO 27001, the Essential Eight), security tools, configuring controls, vulnerability management and cloud security basics.
Grow the lab

Add a deliberately vulnerable VM, such as Metasploitable 2, on the internal network only. Add a SIEM, such as Wazuh (give it 4 to 8 GB of RAM), and send it Windows and Linux logs. Then attack your lab and detect yourself.
Show your work

Write up each lab on GitHub: goal, setup, steps, what you saw and what you'd fix. Screenshots and clear explanations beat a list of courses. Never publish real credentials or anything from an employer's systems.
Certifications

CompTIA Security+ is a common first security certification and often appears in entry-level job ads. For cloud roles, start with an entry cert like AWS Cloud Practitioner or Microsoft SC-900, then aim for a cloud security cert. Pair any cert with lab write-ups.
Keep the habit
A few cards a day beats a cram. Redo red days in the Days picker. Follow alerts from Australia's ACSC and New Zealand's NCSC, and read one incident write-up a week.
real: What hiring managers look for

Entry-level security roles usually want networking and OS basics, log analysis, some scripting and clear communication. IT support is a real asset: you already troubleshoot, document and calm down stressed users. Say that in interviews, with examples.
myth: Certifications alone will get you hired.
They help you get past filters, but interviews test whether you can do and explain the work. Documented lab projects prove that.

tryit.p: Create a public repo called homelab and add a README for your Day 25 lab using this outline. Keep it short and use screenshots from your own lab only.
tryit.code:
# Lab 01: Scan and watch
## Goal
Detect an Nmap SYN scan from the defender's side.
## Setup
VirtualBox internal network. Kali 10.10.10.10, Windows 10.10.10.20.
## Steps
## What I saw
## What I'd change in a real network

quiz.q: What's the strongest evidence of skill for an employer?
quiz.w: Write-ups of real lab work show what you can do, not just what you've read.

quiz.q: Where should Metasploitable 2 be connected in your lab?
o: NAT with ports forwarded from the internet
quiz.w: It's deliberately full of holes. It must never be reachable from your home network or the internet.

quiz.q: Which of these should never go in a public lab write-up?
o: Real credentials or details from an employer's systems
What you'd do differently next time
quiz.w: Publishing real credentials or work details is a breach in its own right. Keep write-ups to your own lab.

quiz.q: What does a SIEM add to your lab?
quiz.w: A SIEM lets you practise the defender's job: collecting logs, writing detections and responding to alerts.

recap: Stage 1 done: fundamentals, networking, OS, crypto, hands-on analysis.
Grow the lab with a vulnerable VM and a SIEM, kept internal.
Write up everything on GitHub.
Next: the intermediate stage.

days.sub: The identity system behind Microsoft 365 and Azure.
learn: What it is

Microsoft Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud identity service, called Azure Active Directory until 2023. It holds the users, groups, devices and apps for Microsoft 365 and Azure, and handles their sign-ins.
Not AD in the cloud

On-premises Active Directory uses Kerberos, NTLM and LDAP, with OUs and Group Policy. Entra ID uses web protocols such as OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect and SAML. Many organisations run both and sync accounts with Microsoft Entra Connect.
Roles

Admin rights come from roles. Global Administrator can change almost anything, so Microsoft recommends fewer than five of them. Narrower roles, such as User Administrator, Helpdesk Administrator and Security Reader, cover most day-to-day work.
Just-in-time admin

Privileged Identity Management (PIM) lets people activate an admin role only when they need it, for a few hours, with MFA and optionally approval. Few people then hold standing admin rights an attacker could steal. PIM needs Entra ID P2 or Entra ID Governance licences.
Apps are identities too

Enterprise applications and service principals sign in and get permissions too. An app granted broad access to mail or files is as valuable to an attacker as an admin account, so review app permissions as well as people.
real: Midnight Blizzard and Microsoft, 2024

In January 2024 Microsoft disclosed that a Russian state group had password-sprayed a legacy test tenant account with no MFA. The attackers then abused an old test OAuth app with elevated access to reach email belonging to senior leaders and security staff.
myth: Entra ID is just Active Directory in the cloud.
It's a different system with different protocols, no OUs and no Group Policy. Many skills transfer, but cloud identity has its own attacks, like consent phishing and token theft.

tryit.p: Use Microsoft Graph PowerShell in a tenant you own, such as a free trial. This lists the roles switched on in your tenant, then who actively holds one. People only eligible through PIM won't appear.
tryit.code:
Install-Module Microsoft.Graph -Scope CurrentUser
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "RoleManagement.Read.Directory"
Get-MgDirectoryRole | Select-Object DisplayName, Id
Get-MgDirectoryRoleMember -DirectoryRoleId <role-id>

quiz.q: What was Microsoft Entra ID called before 2023?
quiz.w: Microsoft renamed Azure AD to Microsoft Entra ID in 2023. The service itself didn't change.

quiz.q: How many Global Administrators does Microsoft recommend?
quiz.w: Global Administrator can change almost anything. Keep it to a few people and give everyone else narrower roles.

quiz.q: What does Privileged Identity Management (PIM) add?
o: Admin roles that are activated only when needed, for a limited time
A second copy of every user account
quiz.w: Just-in-time access means far fewer permanent admin rights waiting to be stolen.

quiz.q: How did the attackers first get into Microsoft in the 2024 Midnight Blizzard incident?
o: Password spraying a legacy test account that had no MFA
quiz.w: A forgotten, low-value test account without MFA became the way in. Old accounts and apps need the same controls as new ones.

recap: Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud identity service, formerly Azure AD.
It uses OAuth, OpenID Connect and SAML, not Kerberos and LDAP.
Keep Global Administrators to a few; use PIM for just-in-time admin.
Apps and service principals need permission reviews too.

days.sub: If this sign-in looks like that, then require this.
learn: If, then

Conditional Access policies are if-then rules for sign-ins. If the user, app, location, device or risk matches, then block, allow, or require something extra such as MFA or a compliant device. Risk-based conditions need Entra ID P2.
When it runs

Conditional Access is checked after the first sign-in step, when Entra ID knows who is signing in. It needs Entra ID P1 licences; tenants without them can turn on security defaults, which require MFA in a simpler, all-or-nothing way.
Test before you enforce
Every new policy can run in report-only mode first. Sign-in logs then show what would have happened, so you can catch a policy that would lock out a whole team before it does.
Block legacy authentication
Old protocols, like basic authentication for email, can't do MFA, so password sprays target them. A policy that blocks legacy authentication closes that gap.
Emergency access accounts

Keep at least two cloud-only break-glass accounts excluded from your Conditional Access policies, protected by phishing-resistant MFA such as FIDO2 keys kept somewhere safe. Alert on every use. They save you if a bad policy locks everyone else out.
real: One setting, huge effect

In 2019 Microsoft reported that MFA would block over 99.9% of automated attacks on accounts. Conditional Access is how most organisations require it in the right places, and block the legacy protocols that can't use it.
myth: Conditional Access replaces MFA.
It decides when to require MFA and what else to check. Without MFA or a phishing-resistant method behind it, there's nothing strong to require.

tryit.p: In your own test tenant, open Conditional Access (under Entra ID or Protection, depending on your portal version). Create a policy that requires MFA for a test user, set it to report-only, sign in as that user, then check the sign-in log's Conditional Access details. Exclude your emergency account from every policy.

quiz.q: What's the best way to test a new Conditional Access policy?
o: Report-only mode, then check the sign-in logs
Turn it on for everyone and wait for complaints
Test it on the Global Administrator first
quiz.w: Report-only shows what would happen without blocking anyone.

quiz.q: Why block legacy authentication?
o: It can't do MFA, so password sprays target it
quiz.w: An MFA policy doesn't help if attackers can sign in through a protocol that never asks for MFA.

quiz.q: What are emergency access (break-glass) accounts for?
o: Getting back in if a policy or outage locks everyone out
quiz.w: They're excluded from Conditional Access policies but still protected with phishing-resistant MFA and monitored, so any use is a big deal.

quiz.q: A small business has no Entra ID P1 licences. What's the simplest way to require MFA?
o: Write a Conditional Access policy anyway
quiz.w: Conditional Access needs P1. Security defaults give free, baseline MFA for everyone.

recap: Conditional Access is if-then rules for sign-ins.
It needs P1; security defaults are the free baseline.
Test in report-only, block legacy authentication.
Keep two monitored break-glass accounts outside the policies.

days.sub: Two permission systems, often confused.
learn: Two systems

Entra roles control the directory: users, groups, apps and tenant settings. Azure role-based access control (RBAC) controls Azure resources, like virtual machines, storage and networks. Being powerful in one doesn't automatically make you powerful in the other.
Scopes
Azure RBAC is assigned at a scope: management group, subscription, resource group or a single resource. Assignments flow down, so Owner on a subscription means Owner on everything inside it.
The built-in roles

Owner can manage everything, including granting access. Contributor can create and change resources but can't grant access. Reader can only look. These manage resources, not the data inside: reading blobs needs a data role such as Storage Blob Data Reader.
An assignment has three parts
A role assignment links a security principal (a user, group or app), a role definition, and a scope. Assign roles to groups, not individuals, at the narrowest scope that works.
Global Admin and Azure
A Global Administrator doesn't control Azure subscriptions by default, but can elevate themselves to User Access Administrator over all of them. That switch is logged and should alert.
real: Owner to save time

A common finding in cloud reviews: a contractor given Owner on a whole subscription “to save time”. They could grant access to anyone and delete anything. Contributor on one resource group would have done the job.
myth: Global Administrator automatically controls every Azure subscription.
Not by default. They can elevate themselves to manage access across all subscriptions, which is why that action should be logged and alerted on.

tryit.p: List every role assignment for a user across all scopes, then read what a built-in role allows. Look for Owner where Contributor or Reader would do.
tryit.code:
az login
az role assignment list --assignee user@example.com --all --output table
az role definition list --name Contributor --output json

quiz.q: Which permission system controls who can manage Azure virtual machines?
quiz.w: Azure resources use Azure RBAC. Entra roles control the directory itself.

quiz.q: What can Owner do that Contributor can't?
quiz.w: Contributor manages resources but not access. Owner manages both.

quiz.q: Someone is Reader on a subscription. What can they do in a resource group inside it?
o: Read it, because assignments flow down
quiz.w: Assignments at a higher scope are inherited by everything below.

quiz.q: A contractor needs to manage one app's resources. What's the best assignment?
o: Contributor on that app's resource group
quiz.w: Narrowest role, narrowest scope. Contributor can't grant access, and the resource group limits the reach.

recap: Entra roles run the directory; Azure RBAC runs resources.
Scopes run from management group to resource, and inherit down.
Owner grants access; Contributor can't; Reader only reads.
Assign to groups at the narrowest scope.

days.sub: What an EDR sees, and what it lets you do.
learn: EDR, not just antivirus

Antivirus blocks known bad files. Endpoint detection and response (EDR) records what processes, files, network connections and logons do, so you can spot suspicious behaviour and investigate it. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint is a common example. Its attack surface reduction rules, like blocking Office apps from creating child processes, stop common attack steps outright.
Alerts become incidents
Defender groups related alerts into incidents in the Microsoft Defender portal. One incident might combine a phishing email, a malicious document and a PowerShell download across several devices.
The device timeline
Each device has a timeline and process tree. You can follow exactly what happened: Word started PowerShell, which connected to an IP, which downloaded a file.
Response actions

From the portal you can isolate a device from the network, run an antivirus scan, collect an investigation package or use live response. Isolation keeps the device connected to Defender, so you can keep investigating.
Advanced hunting
Advanced hunting runs KQL over tables like DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceNetworkEvents and DeviceLogonEvents, with 30 days of data. It's how you ask “has this happened anywhere else?”
real: A typical SOC alert

An analyst gets “Suspicious PowerShell command line” on a finance laptop. The process tree shows Word as the parent. They isolate the device, check advanced hunting for the same command on other devices, and find one more. Both are contained within minutes.
myth: EDR is just antivirus with a new name.
Antivirus mostly blocks known files. EDR records behaviour so you can detect new techniques, investigate what happened and respond across devices.

tryit.p: If you have access to a Defender trial or lab, run this to find devices and accounts with many failed logons in the last day.
tryit.code:
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType == "LogonFailed"
| summarize failures = count() by DeviceName, AccountName
| top 10 by failures

quiz.q: What does EDR add on top of antivirus?
o: A record of device behaviour you can investigate and respond to
A firewall for the whole network
quiz.w: EDR is about visibility and response, not just blocking known files.

quiz.q: Why isolate a device instead of switching it off?
o: It stops the spread but keeps evidence and the Defender connection
It's faster to switch on later
quiz.w: An isolated device can't reach the network but can still be investigated, and memory evidence survives.

quiz.q: Which table records process launches in advanced hunting?
quiz.w: DeviceProcessEvents holds process creation, including command lines and parent processes.

quiz.q: You find one device running a malicious command. What's the best next question?
o: Has this command run on any other device?
quiz.w: Scope comes next. Advanced hunting across all devices tells you how far it has spread.

recap: EDR records behaviour; antivirus blocks known files.
Alerts are grouped into incidents in the Defender portal.
Isolate devices to contain them without losing evidence.
Advanced hunting uses KQL across Device tables.

days.sub: From log to alert to closed incident.
learn: What Sentinel is
Microsoft Sentinel is a cloud SIEM and SOAR built on a Log Analytics workspace. It's moving fully into the Microsoft Defender portal: Sentinel in the Azure portal is due to retire on 31 March 2027.
How alerts are made

Data connectors bring in logs from Entra ID, Defender, firewalls and more. Analytics rules, usually scheduled KQL queries, look for suspicious patterns and raise alerts, which are grouped into incidents.
Entities
Alerts map entities such as accounts, hosts and IP addresses. Clicking an entity shows everything Sentinel knows about it, which makes linking related activity much faster.
Working an incident

Assign yourself, set it to Active, check the severity, investigate the entities and evidence, then close it with a classification: true positive, benign positive, false positive or undetermined. The Defender portal words them slightly differently. Good notes help the next analyst.
Automation

Automation rules can assign, tag or close incidents. Playbooks, built on Azure Logic Apps, can take actions like disabling a user or posting to Teams. Automate the repetitive steps; keep people for judgement.
real: Tuning the noise

A new SOC turns on dozens of analytics rules and gets hundreds of incidents a day, most benign. Analysts start skimming. Tuning the noisiest rules with exclusions and thresholds is what lets the real incidents stand out.
myth: More analytics rules always means better detection.
Untuned rules create alert fatigue, and real attacks get missed in the noise. Fewer, well-tuned rules beat many noisy ones.

tryit.p: Open Microsoft's free Log Analytics demo environment (it may ask you to sign in) and try a summary query. If this table is empty or missing, pick another from the list on the left and adapt it.
tryit.code:
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| summarize events = count() by EventID
| top 10 by events

quiz.q: What turns a KQL query into alerts in Sentinel?
quiz.w: Connectors bring data in, workbooks visualise it, and analytics rules detect and alert.

quiz.q: An incident turns out to be a real admin doing approved work. How should it be closed?
quiz.w: The detection was right, the activity happened, but it wasn't malicious. That's a benign positive.

quiz.q: What are Sentinel playbooks built on?
quiz.w: Playbooks are Logic Apps workflows that can take response actions automatically or on demand.

quiz.q: Analysts are ignoring incidents because most are noise. What's the best fix?
quiz.w: Alert fatigue is a tuning problem. Fewer, better alerts get real attention.

recap: Sentinel is a cloud SIEM and SOAR on Log Analytics.
Connectors bring data; analytics rules raise alerts; incidents group them.
Close with true positive, benign positive or false positive.
Tune rules to beat alert fatigue.

days.sub: Which of ten thousand findings do you fix first?
learn: CVEs
A CVE ID, like CVE-2021-44228, names one publicly known vulnerability. Scanners match the software and versions you run against CVEs, and often return thousands of findings.
CVSS: how bad

The Common Vulnerability Scoring System rates severity from 0 to 10. Under CVSS v3, 9.0 and above is critical, 7.0 to 8.9 high, 4.0 to 6.9 medium, 0.1 to 3.9 low and 0.0 none. CVSS v4.0 came out in 2023.
EPSS: how likely

The Exploit Prediction Scoring System, from FIRST, estimates the probability that a vulnerability will be exploited in the next 30 days. A medium CVSS flaw with a high EPSS can matter more than a critical one nobody exploits.
KEV: already happening
CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue lists flaws attackers are using in the wild. If something you run is on it, especially if it's internet-facing, it goes to the top of the list.
Putting it together

Fix internet-facing systems with known or likely exploitation first. The Essential Eight asks for internet-facing services to be patched within 48 hours when the vendor rates a flaw critical or a working exploit exists, and within two weeks otherwise.
real: Citrix Bleed, 2023

CVE-2023-4966 in Citrix NetScaler leaked session tokens. It was exploited as a zero-day from late August 2023, before the October patch. Patching stopped new leaks, but stolen sessions kept working, so Citrix told customers to kill all active sessions too. Ransomware groups used it against large organisations.
myth: Always patch the highest CVSS score first.
Severity isn't likelihood. Exposure, exploitation in the wild (KEV) and probability (EPSS) often matter more than the raw score.

tryit.p: Ask FIRST's free EPSS API for a CVE's exploitation probability, then count the entries in CISA's KEV catalogue.
tryit.code:
curl -s "https://api.first.org/data/v1/epss?cve=CVE-2023-4966"

curl -s https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/feeds/known_exploited_vulnerabilities.json |
  python3 -c "import json,sys; print(len(json.load(sys.stdin)['vulnerabilities']), 'known exploited')"

quiz.q: What does EPSS estimate?
o: The probability a vulnerability will be exploited in the next 30 days
How long a patch takes to install
quiz.w: CVSS is severity; EPSS is likelihood of exploitation. Use both.

quiz.q: A flaw in your internet-facing VPN appears in CISA's KEV catalogue. What does that tell you?
o: Attackers are actively exploiting it, so fix it first
It only affects US government systems
quiz.w: KEV means exploitation is happening now. Internet-facing plus KEV goes straight to the top.

quiz.q: Under CVSS v3, what rating does a score of 9.8 get?
quiz.w: 9.0 to 10.0 is critical; 7.0 to 8.9 is high.

quiz.q: Why wasn't patching enough for Citrix Bleed?
o: Session tokens stolen before the patch kept working until sessions were killed
quiz.w: A patch closes the hole, but anything stolen through it stays valid. Revoke sessions, tokens and credentials too.

recap: CVE names the flaw; CVSS rates severity.
EPSS estimates likelihood; KEV confirms exploitation.
Internet-facing plus exploited goes first.
After patching, revoke what may have been stolen.

days.sub: Microsoft and cloud identity, pulled together.
learn: How to review
Answer each review heading out loud before you read it. Then do the quiz without scrolling back. These topics come up often in junior SOC and cloud interviews.
real: Putting the week together

An alert in Sentinel shows a sign-in to a contractor account from a new country without MFA. Conditional Access should have required MFA, the account had Owner on a subscription, and Defender shows a new process on a server. Every topic this week touches that one incident.
myth: Cloud security is a completely different field from what you've learned.
It's the same ideas: identity, least privilege, logging, detection and patching. The names and tools change: Entra roles, RBAC, Conditional Access, Sentinel and Defender.

tryit.p: Use the real-world card's scenario. In half a page, write what you'd check first, which logs you'd query, what you'd contain, and which control would have stopped it. That's an interview answer and a portfolio piece.

review: Entra ID
Microsoft's cloud identity, formerly Azure AD. Web protocols, not Kerberos. Few Global Administrators, PIM for just-in-time admin, and review app permissions too.
Conditional Access
If-then sign-in rules: block, allow, or require MFA or a compliant device. Needs P1; security defaults otherwise. Test in report-only, block legacy auth, keep break-glass accounts.
RBAC versus Entra roles
Entra roles run the directory; Azure RBAC runs resources at inherited scopes. Owner grants access, Contributor can't, Reader reads.
Defender and Sentinel
Defender for Endpoint records device behaviour and lets you isolate and hunt. Sentinel collects logs, raises alerts from analytics rules and groups them into incidents.
Vulnerability management
CVSS is severity, EPSS is likelihood, KEV is confirmed exploitation. Internet-facing and exploited first. Revoke stolen sessions after patching.

quiz.q: Which Microsoft feature can require MFA only for risky or external sign-ins?
quiz.w: Conditional Access applies conditions like location and risk (risk needs P2) before deciding what to require.

quiz.q: A user can create VMs but can't give anyone else access. Which Azure role fits?
quiz.w: Contributor manages resources without managing access.

quiz.q: Which Sentinel component turns a scheduled KQL query into alerts?
quiz.w: Analytics rules detect; connectors ingest; workbooks visualise.

quiz.q: What's the best way to contain a compromised laptop in Defender for Endpoint?
o: Switch it off at the wall
quiz.w: Isolation cuts it off from the network while keeping the evidence and the Defender connection.

quiz.q: Two flaws: CVSS 9.1 with no known exploitation on an internal server, and CVSS 7.5 in KEV on your internet-facing VPN. Which first?
quiz.w: Exposure and active exploitation beat raw severity.

quiz.q: Why keep emergency access accounts outside Conditional Access?
o: So a broken policy can't lock every admin out
So they can skip MFA forever unnoticed
Because Conditional Access can't apply to admins
quiz.w: They're your way back in, so protect them with phishing-resistant MFA and alert on every use.

quiz.q: What did Midnight Blizzard abuse after its first foothold at Microsoft in 2024?
o: An old test OAuth app with elevated access
quiz.w: Apps are identities too. Unused apps with broad permissions are a quiet route to sensitive data.

recap: Identity is the cloud perimeter: Entra ID, Conditional Access, PIM.
Least privilege in Azure: narrow roles at narrow scopes.
Detect with Sentinel, respond with Defender.
Patch by exposure and exploitation, not just score.
